_meta: Two traffic scenarios -- a healthy period with a few transient failures and a widespread outage -- used to show why retries must be capped by a RETRY BUDGET (a bound on retry volume as a fraction of requests) rather than issued on every failure, or a dependency's bad moment turns into a retry storm that piles extra load on it exactly when it is least able to take it. Retrying a failed request is usually right: most failures are transient, and one retry recovers them cheaply. The danger is that a retry is extra load, and when failures stop being rare -- a dependency degrades or goes down and suddenly most requests fail -- retrying every one of them multiplies the load on the struggling dependency at the worst possible time, deepening the outage (a retry storm / metastable failure). Jitter spreads the retries out in time and retrying at only one layer stops them from multiplying across layers, but neither bounds the TOTAL volume: if every failure retries, an outage where 80% fail nearly doubles the offered load. A retry budget fixes this by treating retries as a scarce resource: allow retries only up to a small fraction of the request rate (a token bucket refilled at, say, 10% of requests), and once the budget is spent, fail fast without retrying. The budget is invisible in normal operation, because transient failures are far below it and every one still gets retried; it only bites during a broad outage, capping the amplification. requests is the number of requests in the window; budget_fraction is the retry budget as a fraction of requests; scenarios give, per period, how many of those requests fail (and would be retried). requests, budget_fraction, and scenarios are the fixture; the retry counts, total offered load, and amplification factor with and without the budget are computed.
